question: Which skin layer provides the primary barrier against topical drug absorption?
explanation: The stratum corneum consists of dead, keratinized cells and lipids that block most foreign substances from entering the body. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h1)

question: How does skin hydration affect the absorption of topical medications?

options.A: Hydration has no effect on absorption

explanation: Well-hydrated skin swells and loosens the dense lipid structure of the outer skin layer, allowing medications to penetrate more easily. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h1)

question: What is the primary base composition of a standard medical ointment?
explanation: Ointments are predominantly oil-based semi-solids that create a heavy occlusive barrier on the skin surface. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h2)

question: A patient with a weeping, inflamed skin rash is most appropriate to receive which preparation?
explanation: Creams contain water and oil emulsions that do not trap excessive moisture, making them suitable for weeping skin lesions. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h2)

question: What defines the systemic action of a topical medication?

options.A: The drug stays entirely within the outer epidermis layer
options.B: The drug enters the bloodstream to affect distant organs
options.C: The drug neutralizes skin surface bacteria directly
options.D: The drug only treats the exact spot where it is applied

explanation: Systemic action happens when the drug crosses the skin barrier, reaches dermal capillaries, and circulates throughout the body. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h3)

question: Why are transdermal patches applied to areas with good capillary supply?

options.A: To stop local irritation at the application site
options.B: To keep the skin layer completely dry and scaly
options.C: To prevent the drug from penetrating the skin
options.D: To facilitate rapid entry into systemic circulation

explanation: A rich capillary bed right beneath the skin allows the absorbed drug to be quickly picked up and carried systemically. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h3)

question: Which of the following is an advantage of the topical drug route?

options.B: Requires no skin preparation at all
options.C: Works instantly on deep internal organs

explanation: Topical drugs bypass the liver during initial absorption, which can preserve drug potency compared to the oral route. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h4)

question: A major limitation of applying drugs through the skin is that absorption is often:
explanation: Skin condition, temperature, and thickness make topical drug absorption vary significantly from person to person. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h4)

question: What is the first action a nurse should take before applying a topical medication?

options.A: Wash the patient with harsh surgical soap
options.B: Apply a tight plastic bandage over the skin
options.C: Massage the cream deeply into the muscle
options.D: Inspect the target skin area for integrity

explanation: Inspecting the skin checks for open wounds, irritation, or contraindications before drug contact. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h5)

question: Why must a nurse remove old topical medication before applying a fresh dose?

options.A: To make the skin change color permanently
options.B: To speed up the local cooling process
options.C: To allow air to enter the subcutaneous fat
options.D: To prevent accidental drug buildup and overdose

explanation: Leaving old residue behind can lead to excessive absorption and localized toxicity or skin irritation. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h5)

question: In which direction should a topical cream be smoothed onto the skin?

options.A: Against the natural hair growth grain
options.C: In the direction of hair growth

explanation: Smoothing medication in the direction of hair growth prevents irritation and inflammation of hair follicles. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h6)

question: Why should a nurse use a tongue depressor to remove ointment from a multi-use jar?

options.A: To press the medication deep into the bone marrow
options.B: To measure the exact blood pressure of the patient
options.C: To prevent microbial contamination of the jar contents
options.D: To ensure the ointment changes its chemical pH

explanation: Using a clean applicator prevents fingers from introducing bacteria into the remaining product inside the container. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h6)

question: A patient asks about covering their medicated skin cream with plastic wrap. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Plastic wrap is safe to use with all skin medications
options.B: Wrap it tightly to make the medication work ten times faster
options.C: Do not use occlusive coverings unless specifically ordered
options.D: Cover it with thick cotton wool instead of plastic

explanation: Occlusive dressings trap heat and moisture, dramatically increasing absorption which can lead to systemic toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended instruction for patients using topical medications?

options.A: Rub the medication vigorously into the eyes
options.B: Wash hands thoroughly after every application
options.C: Watch for signs of skin redness or rash
options.D: Apply the dose only as prescribed by the doctor

explanation: Patients must avoid getting topical medications in their eyes because most formulations cause severe irritation. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T16#GNS125_U3_T16_h7)
